talks.summary:
Research Context and Scope

Dr Lindsay Shepherd of Abertay University presents usable-security research on how COVID-19 changed cyber risk. Her work spans eye-tracking of security warnings, gamification, cyber ranges via the Foresight project, and collaboration with Scottish policing researchers.

Pandemic-Driven Threat Surge

From late 2019, scams impersonating authorities such as the WHO rose alongside rapid remote-work adoption. Critical infrastructure including healthcare was targeted internationally, while high-volume “everyday” cybercrime flooded citizens already stressed by lockdown and routine disruption.

Mapping the Attack Timeline

Shepherd’s team reviewed news and blogs—too recent for journals—to chart worldwide attack evolution from China’s initial WHO alert through lockdowns. UK lockdown coincided with sharply rising scams and malware; literature cited roughly 600% attack growth in March 2020 and millions of daily COVID-themed phishing messages blocked by Google.

Forward-Looking Concerns

Hybrid working persists, so pandemic-era security challenges are not fully reversed. Shepherd argues future major disruptions will recur, requiring lessons from this period about human factors such as afternoon fatigue increasing phishing susceptibility.

talks.title: 2022 | Session 2
talks.teaser: Analyzes session 2 - Breakout A Panel Session and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Panel Purpose

Scot Secure hosts a non-technical incident response planning panel. Moderator Jude notes CEOs are judged on breach handling, not merely being attacked, and shares tools attendees can take back.

First Response Steps

Scottish Business Resilience Centre speaker Declan Doyle advises pausing to breathe, scoping whether email or wider IT is affected, and engaging internal or external IT immediately with offline contact details if Teams or email is down.

Roles, Regulators, and Comms

Organizations need named incident leaders for legal, PR, and technical work; cyber-insurance may mandate specific IR firms. UK breaches may require ICO notification within twenty-four hours of discovery and sector regulators such as the FCA. Internal staff messaging must be planned alongside external statements.

Practice and Scottish Support

Plans should be written, exercised like fire drills, and backed by Police Scotland (101) and SBRC's incident line plus Cyber Scotland Partnership templates for contact lists and playbooks.

talks.summary:
Risk as danger and opportunity

OneTrust GRC engineer Jorge Ferrera's Scot-Secure session reframes risk as balancing danger and opportunity—not only loss. Managing risk well can drive revenue, certifications, and recognition; ISO 27001 Annex A links risks to objectives and controls.

Context and measurement

He asks whether organizations assess risk from past incidents, threat intel, or predictive scanning amid heightened ransomware from geopolitical conflict. Shared risk repositories and guidelines align diverse stakeholders who interpret risk differently.

Board communication

Ferrera emphasizes linking risks to business objectives to secure sponsorship, coordinating across lines of defense, and summarizing context for executives so mitigation is actionable. The talk outlines a five-step methodology tying human factors and organizational specifics to measurable risk management.

talks.title: Session 2
talks.teaser: Details session 2 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
## Risk Heat Maps Aren't Enough

This Scot-Secure session challenges how organizations communicate risk. Speakers note that red-yellow-green heat maps are ubiquitous, but stakeholders often lack shared understanding of what probability and impact scores actually mean for the business.

## Context for Decision Makers

A generic "unpatched system" risk means little to executives without tying it to specific business activities, affected processes, and realistic outcomes. Effective risk reporting must translate technical findings into operational language each audience can act on.

## Unified Methodology

The panel warns against every team using different risk matrices or formulas. Organizations should standardize on one methodology—potentially mapped to frameworks like ISO 27001 Annex A—while allowing narrow variants only where truly needed.

## Linking Risks to Controls

Presenters demonstrate linking risks, control types, weightings, and asset inventories in structured registers (even spreadsheets). Mature programs connect identified risks to concrete controls, standards, and implementation priorities rather than stopping at colorful dashboards.
